evals.prompt: I'm head of product at Lattivo, a payroll-data API (private, Series B, about 1,100 self-serve accounts on click-through terms plus roughly 60 enterprise MSAs). Our reps keep promising things from the internal roadmap: last quarter two deals closed on 'SSO group sync by March', which isn't even staffed. The CEO's answer is a public roadmap 'like Stripe's' by the end of next month so everyone works from one page. Our VP Sales is fine with the page but says he won't sign anything that tells reps what they can and can't say to customers, 'that's what managers are for'. Background so you don't need to ask: the MSA has a future-functionality clause and the click-through terms do too; one internal roadmap, owned by me, reshuffled monthly; of 9 items customers were told to expect last year, 3 slipped; we have a changelog and a deprecation process but no preview phases, engineering just tags things 'beta' in Slack when they feel like it; no voting board, feedback comes through support; I can give this maybe 4 hours a month. Design our public roadmap.
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis that the problem is sales governance, a refusal to publish any public posture until the sales leader and CEO sign the citation rule, the Stripe-shaped dated roadmap listed as ineligible with its failing conditions, no ROI claim, and the sales rules and sales-incident baseline that come first.
expectations: Attributes the sales-promises problem to the absence of a single externally sayable roadmap and of a rule governing what customer-facing staff may promise, not to a lack of transparency or of a page
Declines to publish any public posture while the VP Sales refuses to sign the citation rule, removing public postures from the candidate set rather than ranking them lower
Names fixing sales governance first, with no public page, as the first step, and names the signed citation rule as the condition that re-promotes a public posture
States that publishing without the citation rule hands reps a larger catalogue to promise from, so the page amplifies the problem
Requires both the sales leader and the CEO to sign the citation rule
Scopes the citation rule to anyone customer-facing: reps, solutions engineers, customer success, DevRel, and executives on stage
Reads 'like Stripe' as dated quarters, the most demanding posture, and tests it against the four promotion conditions
Names the failing dated-quarters conditions from the given facts: no release phases exist, 3 of 9 told-to-customers items slipped, and finance has not reviewed revenue-recognition exposure
Lists the Stripe-shaped dated roadmap as an ineligible candidate with the conditions that would make it eligible
Makes no return-on-investment claim (no churn, trust or sales-cycle figure) and states that no independent evidence links public roadmaps to those outcomes
Treats the Slack 'beta' tag as an informal flag: it becomes private preview only once access rules are written, and until then appears as a note on the item, not a phase
Includes the rule that a deal depending on an unbuilt feature goes to product for a decision, never to a rep's judgment
Includes the rule that legal and finance approve any roadmap item written into an order form before signature
Sets a sales-incident baseline before launch (roadmap items in new order forms or side letters, roadmap escalations) to compare each quarter

evals.prompt: Orbiflow here (workflow automation API, about 3,000 integrators). Our public roadmap is a GitHub project board. The item 'Webhook replay API' has sat in the 'Q3' column since spring, and engineering just told me it's Q1 at the earliest because replay was starving live delivery in load tests; they're redesigning the queue first. Two enterprise customers have 'webhook replay' written into their order forms, one of them a renewal that closes in six weeks. The plan I've drafted: (1) remove the issue from the board so it stops attracting comments, (2) mention the new timing in next month's newsletter, (3) post it on the status page as a scheduled change so it's official, (4) re-add the issue later as 'Coming Q1!'. Write the customer communication for me.
evals.expected_output: A slip communication that keeps the item on the board with a delayed status, tells the two order-form customers privately first after a legal check, keeps the slip off the status page, and publishes a notice with reason, workaround, phase-capped timing and a condition to revisit.
expectations: Rejects removing the issue from the board; changes the status on the item itself to delayed (or descoped / not planned)
Rejects the newsletter as the first channel for the slip
Has the account owner tell both order-form customers privately, days before any public update
Has legal check the private notice against the order-form terms first, because the slip may trigger notice, credit or termination rights
Rejects posting the slip on the status page, stating a roadmap slip is not an incident
Public notice gives a one-paragraph plain-language reason (replay starving live delivery, queue redesign)
Public notice offers a workaround or alternative to use meanwhile
Rejects re-adding the item as 'Coming Q1!' with no reason and a bare date
Any new timing carries a release phase (for example Q1 - private preview), never a bare quarter
Notifies subscribers, reactors on the item, and every account the briefing log shows saw the item
Keeps the item visible on the board rather than deleting it, and if cancelled keeps it visible for at least one review cycle
Flags that the original bare 'Q3' column without a phase read as general availability to buyers and reps, and recommends capping every date with a phase going forward
States that the order-form entries bind regardless of the page disclaimer
Structures the public notice as: update date and new status, what changed, what this means for you, workaround, what would change this, and a questions or thread link

evals.prompt: Pinnacle Ledger, accounting API. I've exported our Jira roadmap and want to publish it as a GitHub roadmap repo this week, the same list we show enterprise prospects in NDA briefings (there we'll also name the partner, since it's under NDA anyway). The list: PL-301 Fix auth token replay weakness found in SOC 2 audit; PL-287 Sunset v1 ledger endpoints (we haven't told anyone yet); PL-312 Starter plan price increase plus a new Growth tier; PL-298 Native sync with Tarnbrook Bank (they haven't announced); PL-305 Custom SAML attribute mapping for Harrowgate Insurance (promised in their renewal); PL-320 Migrate to Postgres 17 and split the billing service; PL-290 Key rotation v2; PL-315 Bulk export of ledger data to the customer's warehouse; PL-322 Multi-entity consolidation. Format these as roadmap items for the repo.
evals.expected_output: A gated list: security, unannounced deprecation, pricing, partner name, customer-specific commitment and internal plumbing removed or rewritten, surviving items written problem-first with stable IDs and a single discuss link, the same gate applied to NDA briefings, and an edge-case decider recorded.
expectations: Excludes PL-301 (auth token replay weakness) from both the public repo and the NDA briefings because publication tells attackers where the gap is
Excludes PL-287 (v1 sunset) until it is announced through the deprecation process, and links the notice from the item once announced
Excludes PL-312 (price increase and new tier) as pricing and packaging
Replaces the Tarnbrook Bank name with the capability (sync with the customer's bank) until the partner announces, in the NDA briefing as well as the public repo
Excludes PL-305 (Harrowgate SAML mapping) as a customer-specific commitment that belongs in that customer's order form under legal review
Excludes PL-320 (Postgres 17 migration, billing service split) as internal plumbing
Rewrites PL-290 'Key rotation v2' as a problem-first title (for example 'Rotate API keys without downtime')
States that the public roadmap is never the internal roadmap minus a few rows and runs every candidate through the exclusion gate
Applies the same exclusion gate to the NDA briefings, rejecting the plan to show the partner name under NDA
Records who decides edge cases of the gate in the policy
Marks passing items as public in the internal tool rather than maintaining a separate list
Gives each public item a stable ID that survives from exploring to GA, and one discuss link to a feedback channel instead of comments on the item
Checks the Growth tier and any other item that would cannibalize a current plan against the Osborne effect before publication

evals.prompt: I run community at Tessaro, a developer platform for payments orchestration. We have a third-party voting board with about 1,400 open requests nobody has triaged in a year; the top request ('GraphQL API') has 900 votes, nearly all from free-tier accounts. We're launching a public roadmap next month and my plan is: embed the voting board in it, auto-promote the ten most-voted requests into the 'Next' column so people see we listen, shut down the old board the day the new roadmap goes live and start fresh with zero requests, and rank the Later column by vote count going forward. We don't have anyone whose job is triage; I do it when I can. Can you write the launch plan?
evals.expected_output: A launch plan with locked items and one feedback channel, the untriaged board frozen read-only behind a dated notice rather than closed overnight, no vote-driven promotion, votes weighted by segment, community requests labelled apart from plans, and a format-change notice covering open requests.
expectations: Rejects launching with an embedded voting board while no named triage owner and no running feedback loop exist
Recommends locked roadmap items, each linking to one feedback channel, as the default surface
States the three-option ranking explicitly: on effort and value, separate board > reactions on items > locked items; on efficiency, locked items > reactions on items > separate board
Rejects auto-promoting the ten most-voted requests into Next
Treats vote counts as one weighted signal, never the ranking, weighting by segment and account value, and notes that 900 free-tier votes do not stand for paying customers
Labels community requests apart from vendor plans (a Proposed label or equivalent) so a popular request never reads as a plan
Freezes the existing board read-only behind a dated notice pointing to the single feedback channel, instead of closing it
Rejects shutting the old board down on launch day with no notice; any closure needs a dated notice plus a migration or read-only archive of open requests
States that the 1,400 untriaged requests go to the feedback loop and do not gate the roadmap launch
Gives any board that stays open a not planned state with reasons and a named triage owner
Plans the board's exit before launch, naming a forum closed without notice (UserVoice / Office 365) as the expectation-debt write-off to avoid
Writes the transition as a format-change notice: a dated table of what changes, a 'what's not changing' section, and what happens to open requests
Routes per-request triage and dedup to a feedback-loop process rather than designing it inside the roadmap launch plan

evals.prompt: COO at Brightmoor Systems, a private Series C data-pipeline API company, raising again next spring. We're about to publish a dated quarterly roadmap. Counsel is on vacation for three weeks, so I need a review before they're back. Our page disclaimer so far is a paragraph I adapted from a public company's forward-looking-statements boilerplate, the one about 'risks and uncertainties described in our SEC filings' and the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act safe harbor. Our MSA has the 'purchases not contingent on future functionality' clause; the self-serve click-through terms (about 2,000 accounts) don't mention it. Four enterprise order forms name roadmap items by name. We're also planning to drop the roadmap page straight into the investor data room. What needs to change before we launch?
evals.expected_output: A pre-launch legal review: safe-harbor language stripped for a private company and the customer sentence kept, a four-element disclaimer, the self-serve coverage gap and existing order forms handled through counsel and finance, ASC 606 review as a precondition of dated quarters, data-room reuse routed to counsel, and a four-party approval gate.
expectations: Removes the securities safe-harbor and SEC-filings language from the page disclaimer because Brightmoor is a private company
Keeps only the customer sentence from forward-looking-statements practice: purchase decisions should rest on features available today

Disclaimer carries all four elements: informational only, not a commitment or promise to deliver, timing and content may change at the company's discretion, not to be relied on for purchasing decisions
Flags that the MSA clause does not cover the 2,000 self-serve accounts because the click-through terms carry no equivalent
Has counsel decide whether to add the clause to the self-serve terms and to new and renewing contracts, with written sign-off on the residual risk for existing contracts
States that the clause cannot exclude misrepresentation or deceptive-advertising claims in many jurisdictions, so the page's own accuracy stays the residual exposure
Inventories the four order forms naming roadmap items before launch, with counsel and finance reviewing each and the account owner contacting the customer
States that a feature written into an order form binds regardless of the disclaimer and the MSA clause
Brings finance in before publishing dated quarters, naming ASC 606 (IFRS 15 outside US GAAP) and the risk that a dated, specified upgrade becomes a separate performance obligation deferring revenue
Names finance's revenue-recognition review as a precondition of the dated-quarters posture, not an optional follow-up
Routes the investor data-room reuse of the roadmap to counsel rather than approving it
Defers final disclaimer and clause wording to counsel, presenting its output as shapes rather than legal advice
Repeats the disclaimer on the first slide of any NDA briefing deck, not in a footer
Gates publication on explicit approval by product, sales leadership, counsel and finance

evals.prompt: The CEO asked me to look into a public roadmap for our API platform. Where do we start?
evals.expected_output: A single interview question asking why now, offered as multiple choice, with no posture, vocabulary or tool recommended yet.
expectations: Asks a question before proposing anything
Asks exactly one question in the reply
The question asked is the trigger question (why now), not budget, tooling or audience
Offers the trigger as multiple choice including sales promising unbuilt features, customers asking what's coming, a competitor publishing one, transparency as brand, and a slip that hurt trust
Recommends no posture, vocabulary, tool or surface in the reply
Keeps the reply to the question itself, without a preamble walking through the full workflow or listing the postures

evals.prompt: Product lead at Dunmore Analytics, a data-enrichment API. A competitor published a public roadmap last week and leadership wants ours live in three weeks. Everything you'd probably ask: private company, no fundraise planned; customers are mostly banks and insurers on negotiated MSAs whose procurement teams ask for roadmap evidence, plus a smaller self-serve tier; they genuinely plan budgets around our release timing, which is why leadership wants dated quarters. One internal roadmap, I own it, it changes monthly; 1 of 12 items customers were told to expect slipped last year. We run private preview / public preview / GA, have a changelog and a deprecation process. The MSA carries the future-functionality clause, the self-serve terms too, no order forms name roadmap items; sales leadership and the CEO will sign a citation rule. Feedback: a GitHub Discussions category that DevRel triages every week. I can spend about 2 hours a month on upkeep after launch; setup time is whatever fits in three weeks. Finance has never looked at any of this. What should we publish?
evals.expected_output: The four posture rankings stated and re-ranked for an enterprise-heavy audience, NDA briefings bundled with a small public page, dated quarters withheld on the missing finance review with the condition that unlocks it, item count sized from the two-hour budget, the two-review-cycle rule reconciled with the deadline, and two or three candidate bundles with a recommendation.
expectations: States the four posture rankings out loud (effort, value, compliance cost, efficiency) across the six postures, not only a recommendation
Re-ranks for the enterprise-heavy audience: customer briefings move to second on value and third on efficiency
Promotes NDA customer briefings alongside a public page because regulated procurement asks for roadmap evidence, presenting it as a bundle of two rungs
Promotes the direction page or a small horizon roadmap because of the three-week deadline and the two-hour monthly budget, and says which interview answer moved which rung
Withholds dated quarters, naming the missing finance revenue-recognition review as the failing promotion condition even though phases, the low slip rate and budget-planning buyers hold
Names the condition that promotes dated quarters later: finance review of ASC 606 / IFRS 15 exposure

Sizes the public item count from the two-hour budget using the planning assumption of about a quarter hour per item per monthly review (roughly eight items), and says to replace it with the first month's actual time
Flags that publishing only after at least two internal review cycles with decided statuses conflicts with the three-week deadline, and says how to resolve it
Applies the same sales rules to the NDA briefings as to the page: disclaimer on slide one and a briefing log recording account, date, items and attendees
Presents two or three candidate bundles with trade-offs and one recommendation, listing the dated-quarters candidate as ineligible with its missing condition
Argues the decision on stated trade-offs for the competitor trigger, with no claimed ROI
Notes that the weekly-triaged Discussions category promotes the interactive-board rung with DevRel as the named triage owner, while locked items linking to that category stay the default
Names a single owner and a backup with the monthly hours, never 'product' collectively, and shows a last-reviewed date on the page

evals.prompt: Sorrelton (observability API) is relaunching our GitHub roadmap repo and I'm settling the vocabulary. Draft: columns Now / Next / Later, which I'll credit to the book Product Roadmaps Relaunched in the README; 'Next' defined as 'within about two months'; a quarter label on every card including ideas we're still researching, since GitHub's own roadmap puts quarters on in-design items; card titles like 'Rate limiter v3', 'Auth revamp', 'Dashboard 2.0'; anything that won't happen gets removed to keep the board clean; cards get a 'beta' tag whenever engineering says a thing is in beta. And rather than keeping old cards around, each quarter I'll rewrite ROADMAP.md from scratch so it's always current. Sanity-check and finalize the vocabulary.
evals.expected_output: A corrected vocabulary: Now/Next/Later credited correctly, buckets defined by engineering state, dates only from private preview with a phase attached, problem-first titles, a visible not-planned state instead of removals, beta mapped to a note until access rules exist, snapshots instead of a rewritten file, stable IDs, a Proposed label and a changelog close.
expectations: Credits Now / Next / Later to Janna Bastow (ProdPad), not to the book Product Roadmaps Relaunched
Rejects defining Next as 'within about two months'; buckets are defined by engineering state (for example in build with a named owner) so no bucket smuggles in a date
Removes quarter labels from research and in-design cards; dates appear only on items at private preview or later
Caps every date that remains with a phase (for example 'Q1 - private preview')
Acknowledges that GitHub dates in-design items by quarter column and states the stricter rule is this policy's deliberate choice
Rewrites 'Rate limiter v3', 'Auth revamp' and 'Dashboard 2.0' as problem-first titles
Rejects removing cards that won't happen; publishes a visible not planned or cancelled state with a reason, kept for at least one review cycle
Treats the 'beta' tag as an informal flag: it maps to private preview only once access rules are written, and until then is a note on the card, not a phase
Rejects rewriting ROADMAP.md from scratch each quarter; snapshots the roadmap at each review so promises can be compared with delivery
Defines on the page, for each state, what a customer may rely on
Adds a separate label (Proposed or equivalent) for community ideas so they never read as vendor plans
Gives every card a stable ID that survives from exploring to GA
Closes each shipped card with a changelog link (a shipped label or equivalent)

evals.prompt: Head of product at Ashgrove, a contract-data API (private, about 180 enterprise customers on MSAs with the future-functionality clause, almost no self-serve). At our user conference last October the CEO said on stage that multi-region data residency would be live 'in the first half of the year', to about 300 attendees. It's November, it's not built, and nobody has said a word about it. Two renewals that closed since then reference residency in their order forms. The CEO now wants to repair the relationship by shipping a public roadmap page by the end of the month with residency shown as 'Next'. We don't run preview phases yet, we do have a changelog, no voting board, and I have about 6 hours a month for this. How do we get the page out?
evals.expected_output: A plan that communicates the residency slip first as a launch precondition, tells the two order-form customers privately after a legal check, treats the keynote as a committed item, keeps residency undated on any page, adds a citation rule covering executives on stage, and bundles NDA briefings for the enterprise audience without promising the page rebuilds trust.
expectations: Sequences the communication of the residency slip before any roadmap page launches, as a launch precondition
Treats the keynote statement as a committed item under the playbook's definition (customers were told to expect it), not as an informal remark
Applies the slip steps to the pre-page commitment: a status (delayed / descoped / not planned), a one-paragraph reason, a workaround, notification of those who were told, and continued visibility
Has the account owners tell the two renewal customers privately, days before any public statement, after legal checks the notice against their order-form terms
States that adding a roadmap page before the slip is handled multiplies the next slip
Rejects showing residency as Next with any date or GA implication while no release phase exists; if shown, it carries an engineering-state status and no timing
Includes a citation rule covering executives on stage: no dates in keynotes unless the public page shows that date
Makes no claim that the page will rebuild trust, arguing on stated trade-offs instead
Tracks slip rate using the committed-item definition before any promotion to dated quarters
Promotes NDA customer briefings alongside or instead of the page for the enterprise-heavy audience
